title: Burst Balloons
prompt: You are given `n` balloons, indexed from 0 to n-1, where balloon `i` has a value `nums[i]`. You are asked to burst all the balloons. If you burst balloon `i`, you gain `nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right]` coins, where `left` and `right` are the indices adjacent to `i` at the time it is burst (treating out-of-bounds indices as having a value of 1). Return the maximum coins you can collect by bursting all the balloons in some order.
hints: Thinking about which balloon to burst FIRST is hard, because bursting changes who's adjacent to whom. Instead, think about which balloon to burst LAST within a range.

Pad nums with a 1 on both ends. Define dp[l][r] as the max coins obtainable from bursting all balloons strictly between indices l and r (exclusive), assuming l and r themselves are never burst during this subproblem.

For each range (l, r), try every k strictly between them as the LAST balloon burst in that range: once everything else in (l,k) and (k,r) is gone, bursting k scores nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r]. dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r]. Fill by increasing range width.

solution.approach: The key reframe: instead of deciding which balloon to burst first (which changes adjacency unpredictably), decide which balloon is burst LAST within a subrange. Pad nums with a virtual 1 at both ends so boundaries are handled uniformly. Define dp[l][r] as the maximum coins from bursting every balloon strictly between indices l and r, given that l and r survive until everything between them is gone (they act as fixed 'walls'). For a range (l, r), if balloon k (l < k < r) is the LAST one burst inside that range, then at the moment it bursts, its only remaining neighbors are l and r (everything else between l-k and k-r was already cleared), so bursting it yields nums[l] * nums[k] * nums[r], plus whatever was already earned bursting (l,k) and (k,r) independently: dp[l][k] + dp[k][r]. Maximizing over every choice of k gives dp[l][r]. Fill the table by increasing range width so smaller subranges are ready first. The answer is dp[0][n+1] on the padded array.
